One approach is to condition on the selected event, but for complex selection procedures, the resulting conditional distribution can be analytically intractable and require sampling-based methods. Rejection sampling provides a natural baseline: it repeatedly draws from a proposal and retains only samples that reproduce the observed selection. This can be prohibitively expensive when the selection event is rare. We address this computational bottleneck with a pseudo-marginal Markov chain Monte Carlo algorithm that samples from the selective distribution. Using a weak Poincar\'e inequality, we analyze its computational efficiency relative to rejection sampling and identify when it can offer substantial gains. In the classical file-drawer problem, we derive precise computational costs for both methods, illustrating exponential improvement as the selection event becomes increasingly rare. In numerical experiments involving complex selection procedures without tractable conditional distributions, the pseudo-marginal sampler is often hundreds of times more efficient than rejection sampling, while the resulting tests achieve nominal selective Type I error.

nominations.title: Projection-Based Partial Correlation Inference Beyond Sparsity
nominations.authors: Youwu Lin, Zhaojun Zhou, Shuqi Shi, Xianming Sun
nominations.abstract: Valid inference for partial correlation in high-dimensional Gaussian models is challenging when the conditioning variables exhibit dense dependence and conventional sparsity assumptions are inappropriate. We develop a target-specific projection framework for estimating and testing a population partial correlation without requiring coordinate sparsity. A population quadratic criterion characterizes the information retained by a linear reduction and is maximized by a one-dimensional projection. Under a rank-one alignment condition, this optimal projection preserves the original partial correlation. To obtain a feasible procedure, we estimate the optimal direction using diagonal ridge regularization on an independent training sample. Under conditions on regularized effective dimension and target-specific ridge bias, we establish a quantitative direction-estimation rate in the covariance-induced prediction norm. We further show that, under alignment, the induced partial-correlation error is second order in the direction error. These results yield oracle equivalence and asymptotic normality for the feasible split-sample estimator, as well as asymptotically valid testing of the original zero-partial-correlation null. Exact finite-sample \(F\)-calibration holds under the projected null. An explicit coordinate-dense Gaussian model verifies the required rates even when the dimension exceeds the sample size. Numerical experiments illustrate the finite-sample performance of the proposed procedures.

nominations.title: Harnessing collaborative networks for nonparametric quantile learning
nominations.authors: Jinyuan Chang, Yue Wang, Heng Lian, Wen-Xin Zhou
nominations.abstract: Data are increasingly distributed across networked agents that must learn collaboratively without exchanging raw observations or relying on central coordination. Existing decentralized methods largely focus on finite-dimensional models with smooth and strongly convex objectives, leaving nonparametric distributional learning over networks underexplored. We study decentralized nonparametric quantile regression in reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces. The standard kernel estimator is poorly suited to this setting: the check loss is nonsmooth, while its representer theorem formulation requires a global, data-dependent basis whose dimension grows with the total sample size. We reformulate the estimator using convolution smoothing and shared random features, yielding a differentiable objective with a common, data-independent parameterization of substantially lower dimension. We develop a gradient-adjusted alternating direction method of multipliers algorithm that replaces costly local minimization with network-corrected gradient updates, together with a communication-enhanced variant that selectively transmits updates. We establish nonasymptotic error bounds for the smoothed full-kernel and random-feature estimators, showing that the latter attains the full-kernel rate with suitable bandwidth and feature dimension. We also show both algorithms converge linearly to the random-feature consensus estimator. Simulations and a real data application demonstrate competitive predictive accuracy with substantial computational and communication savings.

nominations.title: Prior Probabilities for Constrained Hypotheses: Invariance, Neutrality, and Model Search
nominations.authors: Joris Mulder
nominations.abstract: When testing hypotheses with equality and inequality constraints using Bayes factors, the hypotheses are commonly assigned equal prior probabilities. The resulting posterior probabilities depend on how the analyst divides the parameter space into hypotheses: splitting one hypothesis into two changes the posterior probabilities of the other hypotheses, and a hypothesis can receive more posterior probability than a hypothesis that contains it. An alternative is considered where the prior probabilities of the hypotheses follow from a single prior distribution on the parameters. Prior probabilities of the equality constrained subspaces are taken from the Bayesian variable selection literature, and prior probabilities of the inequality constrained regions within these subspaces are given by their relative complexities under the encompassing prior. Under this complexity-induced prior, posterior probabilities do not depend on how the hypotheses are divided, are coherent across nested hypotheses, and agree with those from an exploratory model search over the same subspaces. In return, inequality constraints do not increase the posterior probability of a hypothesis relative to the null hypothesis. The prior is therefore suited for analysts who want to test constrained hypotheses without favoring specific constraints a priori, while the potential gain in evidence for the constraints remains quantified by the Bayes factor.

nominations.title: Testing isotropy of random fields with values in abstract spaces
nominations.authors: Julius Baumhakel, Siegfried H\"ormann, Matthias Neumann
nominations.abstract: We study the problem of testing isotropy, i.e., distributional invariance under orthogonal transformations, for random fields taking values in abstract spaces. We propose a novel approach based on computing local directional characteristics, which are uniformly distributed under the assumption of isotropy. Our work is motivated by an application in material science, where we are testing the isotropy of function-valued porosity profiles of paper sheets, whose morphology is resolved by $\mu$-CT imaging. While considerably more general, the presented methodology is competitive with existing isotropy tests for real-valued random fields.

nominations.title: A Bayesian approach for checking and estimating block designs in agricultural experiments
nominations.authors: Josefina Lacasa, Ignacio A. Ciampitti, Trevor J. Hefley
nominations.abstract: Spatial blocking is a common technique used in designed agricultural experiments. Spatial blocking, however, requires important assumptions about the spatial dependence patterns in the field. Statistical models of blocked agricultural experiments often show spatial structure in the residuals, suggesting that the original model may benefit from additional assumptions regarding the spatial dependence patterns present in the field. We propose a Bayesian model for checking block membership and estimating spatial patterns missing in the original block design. Our model is particularly motivated by cases with mis-specified blocks. To accomplish this, we embed a regression tree within a Bayesian statistical model to estimate spatial effects with a block-like spatial structure. We illustrate the benefits of our model using simulated data mimicking four typical scenarios we have encountered in our applied experience in agricultural research and using two datasets generated from designed agricultural experiments. We found that our model may serve two purposes: validating the originally designed block layout, or mis-specified block-like spatial structures. Thus, our model provides researchers with a novel tool for analyzing data from designed agricultural experiments.

nominations.title: Convergence and global optimality of Wasserstein--Fisher--Rao descent for Gaussian mixtures
nominations.authors: Xingzhou Wang, Ziyang Jiang, Zheng Li, Mingyan Liu, Yiling Wang, Jingze Yang
nominations.abstract: We study explicit Wasserstein--Fisher--Rao descent for fitting Gaussian location mixtures by nonparametric maximum likelihood. The full sequence converges weakly and has finite length in the bounded-Lipschitz metric throughout the original step-size range. These conclusions hold for any fixed data set in any dimension and any initial probability measure. By an earlier conditional optimality theorem, the limit maximizes the likelihood under full-support initialization. Fix any particle step size in $(0,1]$. Initialize the particles by resampling the observations. For an open set of triples of points in the plane, the probability of convergence to a strictly suboptimal fixed point tends to one exponentially as the particle count grows. Without reweighting, a centered Gaussian initialization can give a strictly suboptimal limit. Every finite iterate has a smooth, strictly positive density. The limit assigns positive mass to a nonglobal local maximum of the associated Gaussian sum. We also give the exact pure-transport limit for a one-dimensional initialization with full support and an atom. An exact finite-dimensional representation preserves the truncated likelihood moments and the retained region's contribution to the current dissipation. This lets us transfer an analytic gradient inequality to the measure trajectory.

nominations.title: Measuring Kaplan--Meier Overestimation Under Competing Risks: Event Ordering, Quantification, and Exact Inference
nominations.authors: Ferran Espuny-Pujol
nominations.abstract: Competing risks arise when individuals may experience multiple mutually exclusive event types. Competing events are frequently treated as censoring and analysed using Kaplan--Meier (KM) methods, which overestimate real-world event risks. While the existence of KM overestimation is well known, its determinants, magnitude, and inferential properties remain poorly characterised. We develop a nonparametric framework that treats competing risks overestimation as a statistical quantity in its own right. We show that competing event frequency alone is insufficient to characterise KM overestimation and develop an event ordering theory describing how temporal event allocation influences overestimation. Based on these results, we derive a closed-form Total Overestimation Diagnostic (TOD) that quantifies total KM overestimation directly from routine survival analysis output. We establish exact error equivalence results for both cause-specific and total overestimation. In particular, Product Limit Error Equivalence shows that inference for TOD reduces exactly to ordinary overall survival estimation. Simulation experiments validate the theoretical results and show that independent censoring primarily affects precision rather than overestimation magnitude. Across six benchmark competing risks datasets, cause-specific overestimation is characterised by both total overestimation and temporal event allocation. These results provide a practical framework for assessing competing risks relevance and determining when cumulative incidence methods should be preferred to na\"ive KM risks. The proposed framework transforms competing risks overestimation from a qualitative warning into a measurable quantity that can be routinely quantified, interpreted, and incorporated into reporting practice.

nominations.title: One Curve, Different Weights: AUC, the Brier Score, Decision-Weighted AUC, and the Policy Youden Index
nominations.authors: Yegor Baranovski
nominations.abstract: AUC and the Brier score are standard summaries of a binary risk score, yet they can rank models differently. We introduce a weighted AUC, AUC$_\pi$, which weights each pair of observations by how differently a decision maker with probability of acting $\pi$ treats them. We show that all three are built on weighted averages of one curve, the Youden index $J(t) = \mathrm{TPR}(t) - \mathrm{FPR}(t)$ across cutoffs $t$, and that the averages differ in the weights they put on the cutoffs. Each weights a cutoff by how much something rises across it: for AUC, the distribution of all scores; for the Brier score, the true probability $\mathbb{E}[Y \mid S]$; for AUC$_\pi$, the decision maker's probability of acting. Up to normalization, AUC$_\pi$ is the Brier skill score of the ideal forecast with its weight moved to the cutoffs the decision maker cares about. We also show that weighting pairs by $|\pi(s) - \pi(s')|$ is, up to scale, the only pair weight fixed in advance that makes a pair-weighted AUC an average of the Youden curve for every score distribution. As a ranking measure, AUC weights every model the same way. Hand (2009) shows that it can also be read as an average over cost thresholds, and in that reading each model weights the thresholds differently. The numerator of AUC$_\pi$, which we call the policy Youden index, is the expected share of class 1 a fixed policy acts on minus the expected share of class 0. It judges every model by the same policy and so avoids this; the full ratio AUC$_\pi$ does not.

nominations.title: Spectral-Domain Information Geometry of Stationary Covariance Models: Gaussian and Elliptical Extensions
nominations.authors: Shu Yang, Dongying Li, Wenxian Yu
nominations.abstract: This paper develops an information-geometric framework for stationary covariance structures. We begin with the infinite-dimensional setting, where stationary covariance structures can be characterized without finite-window boundary effects. By formulating the covariance structure as a bilinear form on a suitable class of test functions, we establish its spectral representation and show how finite-dimensional Toeplitz covariance matrices arise as restrictions to nested observation subspaces. For zero-mean proper complex Gaussian wide-sense stationary (WSS) processes, we show that the normalized finite-dimensional Fisher information converges to a spectral-domain metric. In logarithmic spectral coordinates, this metric becomes the standard $L^2$ inner product, yielding an explicit Fisher--Rao distance that is also recovered as the asymptotic normalized affine-invariant Riemannian distance between Toeplitz covariance matrices. We then extend the framework to elliptical observation models by separating global covariance scale from shape. The shape Fisher information is orthogonal to radial nuisance directions and is characterized by a dimension- and radial-model-dependent coefficient. We derive a condition under which this coefficient converges to its Gaussian value as the observation dimension tends to infinity. The resulting limiting spectral-shape geometry is the centered $L^2$ geometry of log-spectra and is invariant to positive rescaling. Numerical experiments illustrate the theoretical convergence results and the recovery of the Gaussian shape coefficient.

nominations.title: Adaptive local Fr\'echet regression with polyspherical predictors
nominations.authors: Chang Jun Im
nominations.abstract: We study local Fr\'echet regression for responses taking values in a metric space and predictors on a product of spheres of possibly different dimensions. We propose local constant and local linear estimators with factor-specific bandwidths and establish uniform convergence rates. We select sphere factors by comparing cross-fitted prediction risks for the full and leave-one-factor-out models. The procedure consistently recovers the active factor set, and the selected local constant and local linear estimators attain the same uniform convergence rates as if the active factor set were known. For univariate Wasserstein responses supported on a common compact interval, the uniform rate holds without an entropy condition on the response space. Simulations with scalar and spherical responses and analyses of vessel speeds and drifter speed distributions illustrate the methods.

nominations.title: Species sampling priors through exact augmentation
nominations.authors: Rams\'es H. Mena, Christos Merkatas, Theodoros Nicoleris, Carlos E. Rodr\'iguez
nominations.abstract: Discrete random probability measures are central to Bayesian nonparametric mixture modeling and clustering. We show that every proper species sampling process (SSP) admits an exact two-stage finite representation of its sampling law. An almost surely finite index selects an initial set of atoms, and a draw is then made with explicitly reweighted probabilities. A decreasing visibility schedule determines both the reweighting and the index law. Averaging the finite conditional measures over this law recovers each realized SSP on every measurable set. Reversing this identity yields a novel and general method for constructing SSP priors from an index distribution and finite allocation probabilities, rather than specifying the infinite weights directly. We characterize compatibility between prescribed index probabilities, schedules and induced weights, and develop new SSP priors with full weak support using light-tailed, heavy-tailed and multimodal index distributions with suitable priors on their parameters. Within this framework, we couple marginal index laws with conditional weight distributions to construct SSP priors whose weights are invariant under size-biased permutation in their defining order. An example of such family is identified as the normalization of the sum of a gamma completely random measure and an independent compound-Poisson measure with gamma jumps, naturally leading to explicit partition and predictive laws. The joint distribution of the selected label and the finite index also gives exact simulation and recursive reweighting for SSPs. Total-variation bounds and numerical illustrations distinguish prior specification, exact averaging and fixed-level approximation.

nominations.title: Statistical Analysis of the Structure from Noise Phenomenon in Generalized Procrustes Problems
nominations.authors: Jiayang Yin, Shuyang Ling
nominations.abstract: In cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM), observations are highly noisy, and scientists often use reference templates to guide matching, alignment, and averaging to reconstruct the molecular structure. However, these procedures can produce an output resembling the template even when the observations contain only noise, a phenomenon known as Einstein from noise (EfN). This phenomenon has attracted attention in statistics, where simplified observation models involving group actions have been studied to understand the resulting model bias. Characterizing the bias in the full cryo-EM pipeline remains challenging. We study template matching and averaging in the generalized orthogonal Procrustes problem, which provides an analytically tractable setting involving continuous orthogonal group action and lower-dimensional projections of ordered point clouds. We show that, for pure Gaussian noise, the mean of the aligned-and-averaged estimator admits the same left and right singular-vector bases as the template but its singular values may be distorted. This identifies the subspace structure imposed by the template even in the absence of signal. We characterize the singular values and bound their distortion, establish finite-sample operator-norm bounds, and give sufficient sample sizes for the population mean to dominate random fluctuations. In fact, this bias still exists under weak signals: when the template rank is at least the observation dimension, the change from the pure-noise mean is $O(\eta^2)$ in signal amplitude $\eta$. Our results provide an explicit characterization of model bias in a registration problem motivated by cryo-EM and show why averaging more observations can stabilize structure imposed by the template without removing the bias.

nominations.title: First-order asymptotic expansions for spectral convergence of normalized graph Laplacians constructed from samples on manifolds
nominations.authors: Eunseong Bae, Wolfgang Polonik
nominations.abstract: Under i.i.d. uniform sampling from a closed Riemannian manifold embedded in Euclidean space, we derive first-order asymptotic expansions for the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of symmetrically normalized graph Laplacians constructed via Gaussian kernels and provide concentration inequalities for the remainder terms. As a direct consequence, we establish the corresponding weak convergence results. Unlike most related works, our analysis does not impose a multiplicity-one assumption on the eigenvalues, thereby extending the applicability of the framework to general manifolds with potentially nontrivial eigenvalue multiplicities.

nominations.title: Asymptotic Bayes Optimality of Sparse Multiple Testing Procedures under One-Factor Dependence
nominations.authors: Prasenjit Ghosh, Arijit Chakrabarti
nominations.abstract: In this paper, we study sparse multiple testing under a Gaussian two-group model with known one-factor covariance and centered Gaussian signals. We derive a first-order risk expansion for the observed-data Bayes Oracle, including a finite-dimensional loading average for heterogeneous loadings and an explicit limiting constant for homogeneous loadings. Under the stated factor-estimation and signal-calibration conditions, the homogeneous one-factor Oracle has strictly smaller leading risk than its independent-coordinate counterpart; observing the latent factor yields no further first-order reduction. We establish asymptotic Bayes optimality under sparsity (ABOS) for the Maximum Residual Down (MRD) step-down procedure with Gavrilov--Benjamini--Sarkar (GBS) stagewise calibration (MRD--GBS). Uniform control of residual errors along the rejection path permits comparison with a fixed factor-known rule without requiring the rejection paths to coincide. Fixed-residual versions of GBS and Benjamini--Hochberg (BH) attain the same leading risk. We also prove ABOS for the Bayesian Step-Down (BSD) rule when supplied with the true mixture, signal variance, covariance, and loss parameters; this is an Oracle-parameterized result. When the expected signal count grows faster than the logarithm of the reciprocal signal proportion, BSD and the observed-data Oracle disagree on several coordinates negligible in probability relative to the expected signal count, explaining BSD's near-Oracle behavior in companion simulations. The results cover diverging and bounded positive expected signal counts, including every fixed polynomial sparsity rate up to the bounded-count regime, under the stated calibrations. A fixed-dimension simulation illustrates absolute-risk behavior but does not establish ABOS.

nominations.title: Lengthscale Estimation for the Gaussian Kernel and Deterministic Response Functions
nominations.authors: Subhendu Pramanick, Toni Karvonen
nominations.abstract: The uncertainty estimates Gaussian processes output rely on the chosen covariance kernel and its hyperparameters. We study the fixed-domain asymptotics of the maximum likelihood and cross-validation estimators of the lengthscale parameter of the popular infinitely smooth Gaussian kernel when the observations are produced by a fixed univariate response function. No theoretical results for Gaussian lengthscale estimation exist in this setting. We prove lower bounds on the lengthscale estimators that depend on the regularity of the response function, as measured by the rate of decay of its Fourier transform. If the response function lives in the Hilbert space of the Gaussian kernel with lengthscale $\ell$, the lower bounds have a straightforward dependency on $\ell$. For bandlimited functions and functions whose Fourier transforms decay as $\exp(-a \lvert \omega \rvert^\gamma)$ for $a > 0$ and $\gamma > 2$, we prove that the estimators blow up essentially at least as fast as $(\log n)^{(\gamma-2)/(2\gamma)}$ in the number of data points, $n$. Bandlimited functions are identified with $\gamma = \infty$. Unlike analogous results for finitely smooth Mat\'ern kernels, our results make no assumptions on the geometry of the observation points. Numerical experiments illustrate the results.

nominations.title: A linear programming approach to finite copula interpolation
nominations.authors: Matja\v{z} Omladi\v{c}, Martin Vuk, Alja\v{z} Zalar
nominations.abstract: We consider exact and interval-valued interpolation of multivariate copulas at arbitrary finite configurations in the unit cube. We first characterize when the prescribed data are compatible with a quasi-copula and derive explicit extremal quasi-copula envelopes. The copula interpolation problem is thereby reduced to a copula sandwich problem between these envelopes. Restricting them to the canonical rectangular grid generated by the data coordinates yields a finite linear feasibility system whose elementary-volume constraints are encoded by a cell--vertex incidence matrix. Farkas' lemma then identifies the criterion of Omladi\v{c} and Stopar with an explicit certificate of infeasibility. Although this criterion is indexed by infinitely many formal cell combinations, we show that it suffices to test finitely many vertices of a sign-polytopal subdivision. We also extend the construction to $k$-increasing discrete quasi-copulas for $2\leq k\leq d$.

nominations.title: On the geometry of Gaussian Mean Shift Detection
nominations.authors: Pedro Abdalla, Grigoris Paouris, Roman Vershynin
nominations.abstract: We consider the problem of detecting a shift in the mean of a standard Gaussian random vector, where the direction of the shift belongs to an arbitrary subset $T$ of the Euclidean unit sphere. We introduce a correlation functional $\kappa(T)$ and establish a general lower bound on the detection radius in terms of this functional. We identify regularity conditions under which this lower bound is optimal up to an absolute constant. As an application, we recover some well-known results in the literature such as the detection radius for $s$-sparse unit vectors.

nominations.title: Smoothed Least-Absolute Conditional Multidimensional Scaling via Iteratively Reweighted Majorization
nominations.authors: Xiao Ling
nominations.abstract: Conditional multidimensional scaling combines latent coordinates with observed covariates to fit pairwise dissimilarities. We develop a smoothed l1 formulation using the shifted Charbonnier loss. We prove residualwise sharpness of the quadratic loss majorizer, monotonicity, compact containment, and stationarity of noncollapsed accumulation points. A uniform additive bound quantifies approximation to exact least-absolute conditional stress. The experiments use paired contamination, separately calibrated loss parameters, combined-configuration recovery, and direct checks of the theorem's inequalities.

nominations.title: Generalized Cram\'er-Rao Inequalities Associated with $(h,\tau)$-Divergence and $(h,\tau)$-Exponential Family
nominations.authors: Satyajit Dhadumia
nominations.abstract: The Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence and exponential family have laid the foundation for information geometry and have been widely generalized. Using Eguchi's theory, the Fisher information metric can be derived from the KL divergence. Based on this metric, Amari and Nagaoka established an information-geometric proof of the classical Cram\'er-Rao (CR) inequality for finite-support models. Among the various generalizations of the KL divergence, this paper focuses on the $(h,\tau)$-divergence and establishes the associated CR inequality, referred to as the $(h,\tau)$-CR inequality, using information geometry. We also provide a proof of this inequality based on the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality, thereby extending its applicability to models with more general support sets. Under suitable regularity conditions, equality holds in the classical CR inequality if and only if the underlying family is exponential. However, for the $(h,\tau)$-CR inequality, this property does not generally extend to the $(h,\tau)$-exponential family. We therefore establish an attainable CR inequality for this family. This new inequality extends the attainment result of the classical CR inequality by the sufficient statistic of the exponential family to the $(h,\tau)$-exponential family.

nominations.title: Analytic and optimized approximations to the median of the gamma distribution
nominations.authors: Richard F. Lyon
nominations.abstract:
The median $
u_\Gamma(\alpha)$ of the gamma distribution has no closed form, but its behavior at both ends is known: it is asymptotic to $2^{-1/\alpha}e^{-\gamma}$ (with $\gamma$ being the Euler-Mascheroni constant) as the shape parameter $\alpha 	o 0$, and approaches $\alpha - 1/3$ as $\alpha 	o \infty$. We write approximations as interpolations $(1 - g)
u_0 + g
u_\infty$ between two elementary-function bounds or approximations, each exact in one limit, with an interpolator $g(\alpha)$ going from 0 to 1, and compare three such forms: a first one between previously proven bounds, a second ending in an approximation from the beta median that is exact at $\alpha = 1$ but does not quite approach $\alpha - 1/3$ as $\alpha 	o \infty$, and a third one, between bounds proved here, that corrects the large-$\alpha$ end of the second. For each form, the ideal interpolator's slope at 0, approach to 1, and value at $\alpha = 1$ are derived in closed form. Rational interpolators with every coefficient set in closed form from these properties, with no numerical fitting, reach a worst relative error of 0.0011 over all $\alpha > 0$, with absolute error below 0.0002. Fitting some of these or other coefficients numerically to minimize the worst absolute-or-relative error then trades accuracy against complexity: the Pareto frontier reaches 0.000087 with two fitted constants and 0.000041 with five, and from two on uses degree-4 rationals of the second form with no $\alpha^2$ term in the numerator. The proofs that the end functions of the first and third forms are bounds are machine-checked in Lean 4.

nominations.title: Nonparametric Maximum Likelihood Estimation for Mixtures of Logistic Regressions
nominations.authors: Muheng Li, Peize Zhang, Xin Bing
nominations.abstract: Mixtures of logistic regressions provide a flexible framework for modeling binary responses, extending standard logistic regression to accommodate unobserved heterogeneity while retaining an interpretable regression structure. In this paper, we study such models with an unspecified mixing distribution. We analyze a sieve nonparametric maximum likelihood estimator (NPMLE) and derive nonasymptotic bounds on the estimation error of the resulting mixture regression function under both fixed and random designs. Our results reveal an explicit tradeoff between statistical estimation error and the approximation error induced by the sieve radius, from which we derive convergence rates under several tail conditions on the mixing distribution. For computation, we propose a finite-particle algorithm that approximates the sieve NPMLE by optimizing the locations and weights of a finitely supported mixing distribution. The method offers numerical advantages over existing algorithms and comes with rigorous convergence guarantees. For any fixed dataset, we establish global convergence of the likelihood to the restricted NPMLE value when the number of particles exceeds a finite threshold. When the true mixing distribution is finitely supported, we further establish uniform global convergence guarantees and derive error bounds that separate algorithmic and statistical errors. Our analysis also yields a denoising bound for the mixing distribution and an identifiability result that complements existing results in the literature.

nominations.title: Identification, estimation, and robust inference of structural autoregressions for multidimensional data
nominations.authors: Bernhard van der Sluis
nominations.abstract: Many modern datasets such as cross-country panels have a multidimensional structure. Conventional approaches on structural vector autoregressions for identifying structural shocks are not directly suited to these settings where data are naturally organized as matrices or tensors, since the number of parameters grows rapidly and identifying restrictions become hard to impose. We introduce a class of structural autoregressions for multidimensional data that achieves tractability and global identification by assuming a Kronecker structure on the model coefficients. We develop a minimum-distance estimator and establish its asymptotic distribution. To accommodate approximate Kronecker separability, we develop confidence intervals for the structural impulse response functions that are robust to local misspecification, and we show their asymptotic validity. Monte Carlo simulations demonstrate the validity of the asymptotic approximations and good finite-sample performance of the estimator and their (robust) confidence intervals. We illustrate the methods on a country panel dataset to analyze the dynamic and spillover effects of US monetary policy shocks.

nominations.title: Instrumental variables with treatment clusters
nominations.authors: Didier Nibbering, Matthijs Oosterveen, Pedro Luis Silva
nominations.abstract: Many policy evaluations include multiple unordered treatments. A common approach is to aggregate these treatments into clusters and apply instrumental variable (IV) methods at the treatment cluster level: The clusters are treated as binary treatments and the IV assumptions are invoked at the cluster level. This paper shows that IV with treatment clusters identifies a weighted average of local average treatment effects (LATEs) under a set of assumptions at the unclustered treatment level. When data on unclustered treatment choice is available, we propose testable necessary conditions for the causal interpretation of IV with treatment clusters. We illustrate our methods with empirical applications to the causal effects of fields of study aggregated into STEM and non-STEM clusters or eight broad study directions.

nominations.title: Backtesting High-Dimensional Expected Shortfall
nominations.authors: Zaichao Du, Juan Carlos Escanciano, Pei Pei
nominations.abstract: Forecast evaluation increasingly uses high-dimensional predictors, but estimation and regularization of large predictive models can distort conventional backtests. This issue is particularly important for forecasting downside risk, where the signal-to-noise ratio is low. We develop out-of-sample Expected Shortfall (ES) backtests that remove the large first-order bias effects of estimating high-dimensional Value-at-Risk, ES, and the evaluation instrument. In a linear ES specification, the proposed methods are easily implemented as Double Lasso with a tail-size-adjusted score as a generated dependent variable. More generally, we characterize orthogonal ES backtesting moments, and establish oracle equivalence and valid inference under time-series dependence and repeated estimation with overlapping and expanding training windows. Simulations show that conventional backtests can severely overreject ES optimal forecasts, whereas orthogonalization improves size control. An application to downside-growth forecasting for G7 economies finds evidence against a US growth-only ES specification, even though forecast-oriented regularization selects no additional financial predictors. The application also shows that accounting for estimation can change rejection decisions in either direction. These findings highlight the distinct roles of predictive variable selection and backtesting in the evaluation of high-dimensional tail-risk models.

nominations.title: Semiparametric Inference in Panel Data with Interactive and High-dimensional Confounding
nominations.authors: Bin Chen, Yukun Ma, Qiyang Yu
nominations.abstract: This paper develops inference for a low-dimensional treatment coefficient in partially linear panel models with high-dimensional observed covariates and latent interactive confounding. Flexible adjustment for observed covariates can leave correlated factor components in treatment and outcome residuals, invalidating standard double/debiased machine learning (DML). We propose Factor-Augmented DML (FA-DML), which estimates treatment-side and reduced-form factor spaces from first-stage residuals. The estimator combines a feasible double projection with three-fold, unit-level cross-fitting. The double projection controls interactions between the two estimated factor spaces. The separate folds eliminate same-training-unit pairings in the leading disturbance components of the factor-estimation errors. Under fixed factor ranks, pervasive factor signals, strict exogeneity, and joint asymptotics in the number of units N and periods T , FA-DML is first-order equivalent to an infeasible oracle, is asymptotically normal, and admits consistent variance estimation. In the baseline simulation design with strong interactive confounding, FA-DML confidence intervals have coverage close to the nominal level. Standard DML and a two-fold variant that estimates both factor spaces on the same units substantially undercover. In an application to U.S. states, FA-DML finds that a 10% increase in the real minimum wage is associated with a roughly 1.1% lower 50/10 wage ratio. The estimate is stable across control sets and first-stage learners.

nominations.title: Hedging out the HEDGE Bias: Identifying Dynamic Partial-Equilibrium Effects with Panel LP-IV
nominations.authors: Endong Wang, Ren Zhang
nominations.abstract: Cross-sectional designs are widely used to estimate dynamic partial-equilibrium effects of an aggregate treatment. We show analytically that these estimates are biased when exposures to the treatment and to aggregate confounders are correlated or the confounders feed back into the treatment. This paper develops the heterogeneous-exposure local-projection instrumental variables (HELP-IV) framework, which compares units while holding the confounder path fixed by instrumenting the treatment and this path with exposure-weighted shock proxies. We prove that HELP-IV identifies the partial-equilibrium effect. We further extend the framework, with the corresponding inference, to multiple exposure margins and confounders, forward-looking outcomes, and cumulative multipliers. Finally, we apply HELP-IV to state fiscal multipliers and regional stock-wealth effects, where it yields partial-equilibrium effects that are smaller than conventional estimates and deliver different implications when ported to macroeconomic models.

nominations.title: Global Trends and Heterogeneity in Modified Adjusted Net Savings
nominations.authors: Xin Xiao
nominations.abstract: Modified adjusted net savings is a derived weak sustainability indicator obtained by subtracting education expenditure from adjusted net savings (ANS). Because ANS equals net national savings plus education expenditure minus natural-resource depletion and carbon dioxide damage, MANS isolates the savings and depletion components and is useful when education expenditure would otherwise dominate cross-country comparisons. This study documents the global distribution, long-run trends, and cross-country heterogeneity of MANS excluding particulate emission damage over 1990-2021. The accounting base is the World Bank World Development Indicators series NY.ADJ.SVNX.CD, and MANS is constructed by subtracting education expenditure from this series. We combine global maps, aggregate time series, country-level heatmaps, distributional statistics, and income group comparisons. The results show that global MANS has increased substantially in aggregate, but its evolution as a share of nominal GDP has been more volatile and uneven across countries. Per capita MANS and global MANS totals remain concentrated in high-income and large economies, whereas low-income and lower-middle-income groups display persistently lower and more volatile outcomes. Country rankings are highly persistent, and some populous countries exhibit pronounced fluctuations associated with natural-resource dependence and structural change. The study provides a reproducible descriptive benchmark for monitoring sustainable development and highlights the need to interpret MANS in current US dollars alongside income-group and country-specific contexts. The findings are relevant for macroeconomic policy, natural-capital accounting, and the design of sustainability-oriented investment strategies.

nominations.title: Taste or Strategy? Nationalistic Bias and Competitor Penalties in Figure Skating Judging
nominations.authors: Jialin Liu, Shu Shen
nominations.abstract: Many decisions rest on expert panels whose members have ties to some candidates, and favoritism is hard to tell from shared taste or better information. Using a rich dataset from figure skating, we find evidence of a strategic compatriot premium and a targeted penalty on the compatriot's close rivals. The premium falls along a randomly drawn start order and, before 2022/23, rises when close rivals have their own judges on the panel. The penalty grows with the compatriot's placement chances and fades once she is out of contention. A counterfactual analysis shows that these biases can shape close competitions.

nominations.title: Dynamic investment and coordination in teams: Theory and experimental evidence
nominations.authors: David Gill, Victoria Prowse, J. Lucas Reddinger
nominations.abstract: Teamwork requires more than the general skills that team members bring. In successful teams, members invest in team-specific skill or capital that accumulates within the team and raises the return to coordinated production. We provide the first systematic analysis of dynamic investment in such team skill. Adopting a dynamic game approach, we develop a novel theoretical framework where investment in team skill creates persistent benefits but is risky because the benefits depend on successful team coordination. We then take this framework to the laboratory to study empirically the factors that influence dynamic investment in team skill. We find underinvestment compared to the efficient benchmark. However, investment responds strongly to incentives, in line with specific theory-predicted patterns. Pre-registered traits (theory of mind and propensity to coordinate) predict investment and team-level efficiency. We conclude that careful design of team incentives and selection of team members can facilitate the development of team skill.

nominations.title: Optimal Regulation and Information Institutions with Hidden Network Equilibria
nominations.authors: Christian Jaag
nominations.abstract: Aggregate outcomes can conceal network configurations that expose households to uninsurable risk and require different public services. We study a regulator's joint choice of a corrective activity charge and an information institution in a two-population network game. Although aggregate behavior follows an exact stable law, distinct specialization equilibria require different targeted interventions. With purchased Gaussian monitoring, primitive conditions imply a discontinuous switch between strong regulation without purchased information and informed specialization. The regulator may alternatively obtain signed certification or elicit a privately known state through a report backed by committed random audits. We characterize the three institutions' optimized values and the cost thresholds at which credible disclosure replaces government monitoring. The institutional choice also changes optimal regulation: even when certification and truthful reporting reveal the same state, costly audits favor less specialization and a higher corrective charge. This ordering and monotonicity in audit costs hold under an explicit interiority condition without global concavity of the audit problem. The institutional comparison is solved in the benchmark without feedback from anticipated policy, while the policy switch and strict institutional rankings admit local persistence under additional regularity conditions. Results depend on enforceable verification, restrictions on data access, and an explicitly limited institutional menu.

nominations.title: Economic Benefits of Cross-Border Electricity Trade and Domestic Electricity Production in Switzerland
nominations.authors: Benjamin Lietti, Ambra Van Liedekerke, Marino Bucher, Michael Beer, Nicolas Eschenbaum, Reto Foellmi, Blazhe Gjorgiev, Fabian Gottschlich, Giovanni Sansavini, Christian Sch\"utz, Urs Trinkner
nominations.abstract: This paper assesses the economic benefits of cross-border electricity trade in the context of rising energy prices and geopolitical uncertainty. Switzerland provides a particularly compelling case because of its geographical location and limited integration into the EU electricity market. We first use the Nexus-e framework to simulate the generation capacity and transmission grid expansion required under autarky and free-trade scenarios. Based on these capacity configurations, a fundamental power market model simulates wholesale market outcomes under projected demand and generation conditions for 2040. By jointly accounting for consumer and producer surplus, as well as investments in generation capacity and grid infrastructure, we provide a comprehensive assessment of the welfare effects of cross-border electricity trade, leading to an estimated EUR 1.5 billion gain. More specifically, open access to cross-border electricity trade implies a EUR 1.8 billion transfer from largely publicly owned producers to consumers. Finally, we provide an illustrative, non-causal mapping of broader macroeconomic effects. Under a price-convergence assumption, the implied demand adjustment corresponds to a GDP-equivalent effect of approximately EUR 7 billion.

nominations.title: Estimating multidimensional poverty under incomplete data in North Macedonia
nominations.authors: Maja Gerovska Mitev, Viktor Stojkoski
nominations.abstract: Multidimensional Poverty Indices (MPIs) are available for more than 100 countries, but rarely below the national or regional level. Local estimates require knowing how deprivations overlap within households, yet the sources that cover every locality, such as censuses and geospatial data, cannot be linked at the household level. We show how to measure local multidimensional poverty under such incomplete data, using North Macedonia as a case study. Combining settlement-level access to services with municipal census data, we pair an independence-based point estimate with sharp bounds over all joint distributions consistent with the data. We find that, nationally, 5.01 percent of households are multidimensionally poor, with bounds of 2.01 to 17.44 percent. Also, poverty is concentrated in small rural municipalities, which are poorer than nearly all municipalities of the capital city under any dependence structure. Validating our index against official statistics, the Global MPI, and a fieldwork deprivation index indicates that the socio-economic part of the index is consistent with external measures of deprivation, while the geographic part captures a distinct dimension of remoteness. Our approach thus presents a promising way to measure multidimensional poverty at the local level in countries where linked household data are unavailable.

nominations.title: EvoSurv: Evolution-Aware Multimodal Survival Modeling Reveals Complementary Prognostic Signals
nominations.authors: Wei Wang, Po-Yu Liang, Jun Bai
nominations.abstract: Accurate cancer survival prediction remains challenging due to tumor heterogeneity. Although multimodal survival models integrate clinical and molecular data, they often overlook evolutionary information encoded in genomic alterations. To address this gap, we developed eTime, a 38-dimensional evolutionary representation comprising eight feature groups that characterize clonal and subclonal mutation burden, mutational spectra, functional consequences, copy-number alterations, and anoikis-related genomic changes. We further developed EvoSurv, a multimodal survival framework integrating eTime with clinical variables and RNA expression. Across six TCGA cancer cohorts comprising 2,782 patients, EvoSurv achieved the highest mean concordance index (C-index) in all six cancers, averaging 0.663 and outperforming three state-of-the-art survival prediction methods. More importantly, we assessed whether evolutionary features provide additional prognostic information beyond clinical and transcriptomic predictors. eTime remained significantly associated with survival in head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSC) and liver hepatocellular carcinoma (LIHC) after adjustment for clinical variables and RNA-derived risk scores. Feature-group analyses further revealed cancer-specific prognostic patterns. In HNSC, T>G substitutions were associated with increased mortality risk after clinical and molecular adjustment, including in HPV-negative patients, with supporting evidence from an independent CPTAC-HNSCC cohort. Overall, these findings demonstrate that eTime captures survival-associated evolutionary information and highlight its potential to provide prognostic value beyond clinical and transcriptomic predictors.

nominations.title: The Dose Makes the Poison: Exposure-Aware Evaluation of Generative Drug Design
nominations.authors: Maria Franz, N. Benjamin Erichson
nominations.abstract: Generative models are increasingly used to propose molecules for drug discovery. They can produce far more candidates than can be experimentally tested, making computational selection essential. Most selection methods rely on predicted molecular properties, such as potency and toxicity, but overlook how these properties translate into drug exposure at a given dose. As a result, molecules that appear promising on paper may require impractical doses or raise safety concerns. We investigate this gap by using physiologically based pharmacokinetic (PBPK) simulations to re-evaluate molecules selected from three PARP1-targeted generative pipelines. Of 60 shortlisted molecules, seven fail to achieve sufficient target exposure, while 28% of the remaining candidates show predicted safety risks at their required dose. Moreover, 85% of candidates with an achievable dose are outperformed by molecules overlooked during static selection. These findings suggest that accounting for dose and exposure can substantially change which generated molecules are considered promising for drug development.

nominations.title: Benchmarking large language models for parameter-level structural identifiability classification in epidemic ODE models
nominations.authors: Geunsoo Jang, K. Sel\c{c}uk Candan, Gerardo Chowell
nominations.abstract: Structural identifiability determines whether unknown parameters can be uniquely recovered from ideal model outputs, making it a prerequisite for interpreting parameter estimates. We evaluated whether large language models (LLMs) can reliably provide preliminary structural identifiability classifications for epidemic models. We constructed a retrospective benchmark of 88 scenarios from 14 of the 27 studies considered, encompassing 696 parameter-level formal reference classifications from published results or Julia-based symbolic analysis. Scenarios were evaluated using Domain-Aware and canonically relabeled ("Domain-Anonymized") prompts, with ten runs per configuration and prompt condition. Six configurations completed all scheduled responses, yielding 83,520 parameter-level decisions for the primary comparison. GPT-5.5 Instant and GPT-5.5 Thinking Medium had the highest accuracies among complete configurations (88.71% and 88.07%). Canonical relabeling improved both configurations and attenuated their performance decline in scenarios with many unknown parameters or state variables, although effects differed across model families. Locally identifiable parameters were the most difficult class (highest strict recall among complete configurations: 42.00%), although the local reference set was small. In multivariable analysis, each additional unknown parameter reduced the odds of correct classification (OR 0.881; 95% CI 0.852-0.910), whereas additional observed outputs increased them (OR 1.666; 95% CI 1.503-1.846). Exploratory evaluations indicated strong performance for GPT-5.5 Thinking High and Claude Opus 5, despite incomplete coverage. LLMs may generate preliminary hypotheses or flag cases for formal review, provided outputs are checked against published results or formal symbolic methods. They should not be used to certify the structural identifiability of a complete model.

nominations.title: STAR: Semantic-Criticality Tiered Allocation of Radio Resources via Zero-Shot Learning
nominations.authors: Albert Shaju, Christo Kurisummoottil Thomas, Mingzhe Chen
nominations.abstract: In remote inference, edge devices transmit high-resolution images over wireless links to a receiver, where an artificial intelligence (AI) model answers task-specific questions about these images to enable reliable decisions. These answers are often determined by a small set of task-causal pixels, such as those of text, whose corruption changes the answer, so these pixels must be delivered with high fidelity. Conventional transmission protects every pixel equally, so it either consumes many resource elements (REs) or corrupts these regions at low signal-to-noise ratio (SNR). To overcome these limitations, in this paper, a zero-shot, domain-agnostic framework, termed semantic-criticality tiered allocation of resources (STAR), is proposed. In particular, a per-pixel semantic-criticality indicator (SCI) is derived from the attention of a frozen vision-language model, so new tasks and domains are handled by changing only the prompt, without retraining. The resulting task causality-aware resource allocation problem over protection tiers is solved exactly by a threshold rule on the SCI, realized by a coded tier for the task-causal pixels and an uncoded, downsampled base layer for the full image. Simulations over a 5G New Radio link demonstrate that STAR attains a semantic accuracy of at least 0.98 for $E_s/N_0 \geq -4$ dB and, at comparable semantic reliability, reduces the REs of robust coded transmission by 59.5% and 91.5% on factory- and vehicle-monitoring datasets, respectively, the latter without any change to the models. Although a deep joint source-channel coding baseline uses fewer REs at comparable semantic accuracy, it must be retrained with labeled data for every new task or domain.

nominations.title: Thickness-Field-Excited Bimorph Piezoelectric Micromachined Ultrasonic Transducer in Submicrometer Thin-Film Lithium Niobate
nominations.authors: Vakhtang Chulukhadze, Jiajun Huang, Zihuan Liu, Will Leskowitz, Tzu-Hsuan Hsu, Yuchen Ma, Udit Rawat, Yao Yu, Bichoy Bahr, Neal A. Hall, Ruochen Lu
nominations.abstract: This work presents the first demonstration of a submicrometer-thick thickness-field-excited (TFE) lithium niobate (LN) flexural-mode piezoelectric micromachined ultrasonic transducer (PMUT). A 670-nm-thick bilayer periodically poled piezoelectric film (P3F) 128Y LN is used to demonstrate a suspended membrane with an area of 0.25 mm$^{2}$, achieving a low resonance frequency of 33.4 kHz for airborne transduction. Its electrical measurements reveal an extracted effective electromechanical coupling efficiency ($k_{\mathrm{eff}}^{2}$) of 3% and a moderate static capacitance $C_0$ of 17 pF. Meanwhile, mechanical measurements using a laser Doppler vibrometer (LDV) yield a high quasi-static peak out-of-plane displacement ($\xi_{\mathrm{static}}$) of 145 nm/V and a high corresponding open-circuit sensitivity ($S_{\mathrm{OC}}$) of 1.4 mV/Pa in the audio band. The fabricated device is compared with state-of-the-art (SoA) airborne piezoelectric transducers with sub-100-kHz resonance frequencies, underscoring the potential of the TFE P3F LN transducer platform by simultaneously demonstrating strong actuation capability while featuring high sensitivity.

nominations.title: Design and Over-the-Air Evaluation of a Digital Twin-Driven Site-Specific Neural Receiver for 5G NR on NVIDIA DGX Spark
nominations.authors: Qiuyuan Chen, Chengyang Yao, Liuchang Zhuo, Yuquan Sun, Cunhua Pan, Hong Ren, Jiangzhou Wang
nominations.abstract: We design and evaluate a site-specific neural receiver for the 5G New Radio (NR) uplink. A corridor digital twin built from a radar scan and refined manually provides 28,671 ray-traced channel records for training an eight-round convolutional graph neural network with pilot-aware inputs and auxiliary channel supervision. The GPU on NVIDIA DGX Spark evaluates time--frequency convolutions in parallel across the received grid to accelerate inference. The receiver uses the standard NR uplink waveform and reference signals and feeds soft bits to the existing transport-block decoder. In over-the-air tests with NI USRP B210 radios under common radio settings, the site-trained receiver achieves the highest mean uplink rate at all five positions. At a non-line-of-sight corner, it reaches 16.2 Mb/s, compared with 4.1 Mb/s for the conventional receiver and 2.4 Mb/s for the 3GPP-trained neural receiver. These results demonstrate the feasibility of integrating neural reception into the 5G NR physical layer and show its potential for AI-RAN deployments.

nominations.title: Joint Air Corridor and BS Coverage Planning for Large-Scale High-Density Low-Altitude Aerial Networks via Channel Knowledge Maps
nominations.authors: Jiaxuan Li, Yilong Chen, Yuan Guo, Fan Liu, Jie Xu
nominations.abstract: This paper studies the joint air corridor and base station (BS) coverage planning problem for high-density low-altitude aerial networks supported by terrestrial cellular infrastructures. In the considered system, unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) operate within a structured air corridor planned over a grid-based airspace, and each BS serves selected corridor grid cells by sharing its communication resources among all UAVs therein. Each BS's traffic load depends on both the number of covered corridor cells and the UAV density, thereby affecting the communication rate available to each UAV. We exploit the channel knowledge map (CKM) to characterize the channel gains between BSs and candidate airspace cells and evaluate desired signals and inter-cell interference for environment-aware offline planning. Based on CKM, we jointly optimize the corridor layout and BS coverage to minimize a weighted objective balancing corridor length and the supportable average UAV density along the entire corridor, subject to minimum communication rate requirements for all UAVs along the air corridor. The joint design is formulated as a mixed-integer linear program (MILP), which can be optimally solved using off-the-shelf solvers. For large maps, we develop a scalable suboptimal algorithm based on Lagrangian relaxation and A* search. Specifically, we incorporate BS resource constraints into A* corridor search via Lagrangian relaxation, and then jointly optimize BS coverage and UAV density along the generated corridors under the original rate constraints. Numerical results demonstrate the benefits of the proposed joint design in supporting high-density UAV operations and show that the proposed algorithm obtains high-quality solutions with substantially reduced computation time.

nominations.title: Stability Analysis of Single- and Multi-Snapshot ESPRIT
nominations.authors: Wenchong Huang, Ping Liu
nominations.abstract: Spectral estimation seeks to recover unknown frequencies from $T$ snapshots, each consisting of $\Omega+1$ noisy Fourier measurements. Super-resolution refers to the recovery of frequencies whose minimum separation $\Delta$ is smaller than $1/\Omega$. We establish state-of-the-art stability bounds for single- and multi-snapshot ESPRIT when the frequencies form well-separated clumps, with the largest clump containing $n^\star$ frequencies. In particular, for single-snapshot ESPRIT, our error bound scales as $$ \mathcal{O}(\Omega^{-1}\mathrm{SRF}^{2n^\star-2}\cdot\mathrm{Noise}), $$ where $\mathrm{SRF}:=(\Omega\Delta)^{-1}$ denotes the super-resolution factor, provided that the noise level satisfies $\mathrm{Noise}\lesssim(\Omega\Delta)^{2n^\star-2}$. In comparison with the minimax bounds [arXiv:1904.09186] and the computational resolution limits [arXiv:2003.02917, arXiv:2211.15208], our result shows that single-snapshot ESPRIT achieves the optimal stability scaling in the super-resolution regime. For multi-snapshot ESPRIT, we establish error bounds under both deterministic noise and Gaussian white noise, attaining the best-known SRF dependence under weaker conditions. Numerical experiments corroborate the theoretical error bounds.

nominations.title: Toward Pseudorange-Based PNT with Starlink: A Mock Fused LEO GNSS Implementation
nominations.authors: Samuel C. Morgan, Zacharias M. Komodromos, Wenkai Qin, Andrew Graff, Zachary L. Clements, W. Jeremy Morrison, Todd E. Humphreys
nominations.abstract: We present experimental results from Starlink for pseudorange-based positioning, navigation, and timing (PNT), emulating a system that fuses a primary communications mission with a secondary low-Earth orbit (LEO) PNT mission. Legacy global navigation satellite system (GNSS) constellations faceinherent vulnerabilities and signal limitations, prompting growing interest in broadband LEO constellations---such as SpaceX's Starlink---for resilient PNT. However, opportunistic use of stand-alone Starlink signals fails to achieve GNSS-competitive accuracy due to frame timing irregularities and reliance on uncorrected poor-quality publicly available ephemeris data. To overcome these limitations, we present a mock implementation of a fused LEO GNSS architecture. Our method extracts time-of-arrival observables from live Starlink Ku-band downlinks and pairs them with high-fidelity, beam-specific orbit and clock models distributed as if provided natively by the constellation operator. In a field campaign, and despite constraints imposed by consumer-grade receiver hardware, the method yields 95% error bounds of 2.33 m horizontally (semi-major axis), 3.37 m vertically, and 11.19 ns in timing, with the actual solution errors falling well within these bounds.

nominations.title: Residual-Closed-Loop SAGE-Brent Estimation for Unknown-Order Wideband Underwater Acoustic Channels
nominations.authors: Wenxu Bi, Peng Chen, Wei Wang
nominations.abstract: Grid mismatch in wideband channel estimation leaves structured cancellation residuals after strong-path subtraction. These residuals generate spurious correlation peaks or mask weak arrivals, turning continuous parameter errors into path-count errors. We propose RC-SAGE-Brent, a residual-closed-loop estimator that jointly refines continuous delay-scale parameters and corrects the unknown-order path set. Within each feedback cycle, ambiguity-constrained alternating Brent searches suppress strong-path cancellation residuals. Candidate validation, resolution-constrained pruning, and full-domain residual redetection then revise the active path set. For linear frequency modulation (LFM) probes, an observable signal-to-residual ratio adaptively scales the model-order penalty to mitigate overestimation caused by delay-scale coupling. Theoretical analysis links off-grid parameter errors to local cancellation-residual curvature and weak-path detectability. Factorial ablations, paired comparisons against standard sparse and off-grid estimators, and measured channel replay demonstrate improved path-set recovery and waveform reconstruction while delineating the operational boundaries of the method.

nominations.title: RaGCD: Reliability-Aware 2D-3D Multimodal Generalized Category Discovery
nominations.authors: Junyong Liu
nominations.abstract: Generalized Category Discovery (GCD) aims to recognize known categories while discovering novel ones from partially labeled data. Existing GCD studies primarily focus on unimodal observations or image-text interactions, leaving the complementarity between visual appearance and explicit 3D geometry underexplored. To exploit complementary visual appearance and spatial geometry, we investigate GCD with paired images and point clouds. However, the relative reliability of these modalities varies across samples, so unreliable evidence can compromise both multimodal fusion and cross-modal knowledge transfer. This challenge is particularly pronounced for novel categories, where labeled supervision is unavailable. To address it, we propose RaGCD, a reliability-aware framework for 2D-3D multimodal GCD. Specifically, Reliability-aware Modality Allocation (RMA) combines prediction-derived reliability cues with modality-specific features to adaptively allocate image and point-cloud contributions at the channel level. Reliability-conditioned Alignment (RCA) further reweights feature-level and prediction-level alignment and selects reliable observations for prototype-level alignment, regulating cross-modal interaction according to sample reliability. Extensive experiments on ModelNet40, Washington RGB-D, and ShapeNet-ViPC demonstrate that RaGCD outperforms the compared methods in overall and novel-category clustering accuracy. Ablation studies support the complementary roles of RMA and RCA, while controlled corruption experiments show that modality allocation shifts toward the less corrupted modality. These results support the effectiveness of reliability-aware interaction for category discovery from paired appearance and geometry.

nominations.title: A Faster and Efficient Indoor User Localization Using Bistatic MIMO Radar
nominations.authors: Shadab Anjum, Sourav Banerjee, Neel Kanth Kundu
nominations.abstract: Indoor user localization is essential for applications such as asset tracking, robotic navigation, and smart-building automation where satellite-based positioning is unavailable. Bistatic MIMO radar exploits bistatic range measurements and geometric diversity from distributed antennas, but low-SNR conditions make the resulting estimation ill-conditioned. We formulate indoor localization as a Tikhonov-regularized nonlinear least-squares problem and solve it with a damped Gauss-Newton (DGN) algorithm, in which each iteration reduces to a closed-form 3x3 linear solve followed by an Armijo backtracking line search. Simulations show accuracy on par with, and runtime far faster than, an SDP-based benchmark.

nominations.title: Application of the Phase Correction Method in Tracking Modules of Navigation Receivers
nominations.authors: Kudryavtsev I. A., Shafran S. V., Balmasova M. A
nominations.abstract: One of the problems of the tracking modules is their significant inertia in case of narrow bandwidth, which is desirable to mitigate signal noise. The paper describes a method of phase correction, improving accuracy and dynamic characteristics of the tracking process in GNSS receivers. The pivotal idea of the method supposes correction of the phase deviation between the received signal and its local copy at the end of every integration period. This correction is performed directly over the phase accumulator of a DDS system. This approach reduces inertial effects crucially. Application of phase correction method with narrow filter bandwidth is much more efficient when FLL-assisted PLL tracking is used. It is shown that in this case a separate FLL discriminator is not needed, and the resulting filter structure can be significantly simplified.

nominations.title: Finite Blocklength Performance Analysis of Uplink RSMA with Practical Imperfections
nominations.authors: Farjam Karim, Nurul Huda Mahmood, Arthur Sousa de Sena, Deepak Kumar, Matti Latva-aho
nominations.abstract: Future generations of wireless networks will support massive communication and hyper-reliable low-latency communications, which are fundamental to large-scale Internet of Things (IoT) deployments with stringent performance requirements. To support such diverse and demanding requirements, robust and flexible multiple access schemes are essential. In this work, we develop a comprehensive analytical framework for evaluating uplink rate-splitting multiple access (RSMA) in the finite blocklength regime under realistic non-ideal conditions. Specifically, we derive closed-form expressions for the block error rate (BLER) and goodput, accounting for imperfect channel state information at the receiver (CSIR), imperfect successive interference cancellation (SIC), and hardware impairments. To reflect practical wireless environments, we model the channel using Nakagami-m fading model. Our analysis shows that at lower transmit power levels, imperfect CSIR is the dominant performance-limiting factor, whereas hardware impairments and imperfect SIC become more significant in degrading system performance as the transmit power increases. To further understand the system behavior, we derive asymptotic BLER expressions. We also analyze the impact of rate allocation, demonstrating its critical role in ensuring fairness and reliability. Monte Carlo simulations validate our analytical expressions. Notably, our results show that uplink RSMA significantly outperforms NOMA even when RSMA operates under harsh imperfect CSIR. This superiority establishes RSMA as a robust and efficient candidate for future wireless networks in practical, constrained environments

nominations.title: Dual-Parabola Interpolator: A Low-Bias Peak Estimator for Distributed Radar Synchronization
nominations.authors: Matteo Pardi, Giulio Meucci, Francesco Mancuso, Anna Lisa Saverino, Amerigo Capria
nominations.abstract: Coherent distributed radar processing requires accurate wireless synchronization. Two-way time transfer (TWTT) obtains reception timestamps from sampled matched-filter peaks, but interpolation bias limits accuracy even when noise is reduced by higher signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) or averaging. Three-point parabolic interpolation is attractive for its simple, explicit formula; reducing its bias generally requires more elaborate fitting, such as higher-order polynomials, or a model tailored to a particular peak shape. A practical alternative should retain this simplicity and interpretability while approaching the low bias of more flexible fits. We propose the Dual-Parabola Interpolator (DPI), which combines two parabolic estimates from five amplitude samples near the matched-filter peak. An adaptive weight cancels the leading interpolation error without requiring a waveform-specific peak model or a correction table. Simulations over flat and standardized multipath channels show bias comparable to a five-point quartic fit, with essentially the same standard deviation as the other interpolators and an execution cost close to a three-point parabolic fit. This combination is useful for TWTT in urban or other multipath settings, where channel distortion prevents reliance on a nominal peak shape.

nominations.title: CFAR Detection on Non-Coherently Integrated Angular Maps for mmWave Radio SLAM
nominations.authors: Paolo Tosi, Ossi Kaltiokallio, Marcus Henninger, Silvio Mandelli, Mikko Valkama
nominations.abstract: Reliable multipath detection is essential for millimeter-wave simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM), where propagation paths reflecting off the environment provide geometric constraints beyond the dominant line-of-sight component. This paper develops constant false alarm rate (CFAR)-based detectors for beam-swept bistatic integrated sensing and communications (ISAC). Starting from conventional CFAR on the I/Q datacube, we derive a modified detector for non-coherently integrated angular power maps, where the post-integration noise statistics differ from those assumed by standard cell-averaging CFAR. To improve practicality, we introduce a multi-cell cell-under-test formulation and a plus-shaped training window that reduces computational cost while accounting for sidelobe structure. The proposed methods are evaluated on experimental 60 GHz indoor measurements using a snapshot-SLAM estimator. Compared with a singular value decomposition (SVD)-based detector, the proposed CFAR approaches reduce the overall positioning RMSE from 0.30 m to 0.24-0.26 m, with the largest improvement in non-line-of-sight snapshots. The multi-cell non-coherent detector further lowers the computational complexity without degrading positioning accuracy, demonstrating its suitability for practical multipath radio-SLAM.

nominations.title: Achieving Robust Channel Estimation Neural Networks on Doppler effects by Designed Training Data
nominations.authors: Dianxin Luan, John Thompson
nominations.abstract: Channel estimation is crucial in wireless communication systems. Many existing works train and test their models using the same or similar channel. However, practical channels are infinitely diverse and time-variant while data-driven algorithms often degrade on new and previously unseen channels. This prohibits the practical implementation of neural networks for channel estimation, particularly in high speed scenarios characterized by rapidly channel profile changes and very high Doppler shifts. Online training can fine-tune models to adapt to new channels, but requires high computation resource and incurs significant latency for physical-layer devices. Moreover, online training cannot exhaustively cover all possible channels because there are infinitely many possible channels. Therefore, we investigate the ability of neural networks to generalize to wireless channels. This paper proposes design criteria to generate synthetic training data, which guaranty that the resulting networks perform robustly across wireless channels, especially for very high Doppler shifts and different Doppler spectra. It ensures that offline-trained neural networks require no prior information or online training to precisely estimate the new channels. To demonstrate general applicability, we use neural networks with different levels of complexity to show that the generalization achieved appears to be independent of architecture. From simulation results, neural networks achieve a certain performance across wireless channels with different unseen power delay profiles (PDP) and Doppler shifts.

nominations.title: Time Running Backwards, and Where It Stops: Superoscillations of Proper Time and the Memory of the Environment
nominations.authors: Yakir Aharonov, Avshalom C. Elitzur
nominations.abstract: A quantum system prepared in a superposition of proper times - a clock whose worldline is superposed, or a clock at rest in a superposed gravitational potential - evolves, in each branch, by the same dynamics for a different duration. Post-selecting the control that sets the proper time turns the superposition into a superoscillation of the time-dilation factor: the system is found to have evolved for a proper time $\alpha_w t$, where the weak value $\alpha_w$ may exceed unity, vanish, or be negative - the quantum time-translation machine of Aharonov, Anandan, Popescu and Vaidman. We ask how far back such a machine can run an irreversible process. The test system is a sealed cell - excited atoms, the radiation field they emit into, and the absorbing walls, carried as one quantum object - and the witness is projective: atoms that had begun to decay before the run are found, in the post-selected sub-ensemble, more excited than when inserted. The answer is exact and depends only on the atoms' survival amplitude. With two branches the witness holds only while the decay is younger than the memory time of the environment, after which the emission becomes Markovian. Beyond it, the post-selection amplifies the minute difference between the contents of the cell in the two branches, set by the full energy spread of the atoms and their field rather than by the linewidth, and the witness fails. Reversing a decay past the memory time requires many branches, an environment with a strictly bounded spectrum, and a post-selection probability that falls exponentially with the number of environmental oscillations to be undone. The obstacle to reversal is therefore not entropy but bandwidth - the same bandwidth that makes the emission irreversible in the first place. We give four ways to superpose a clock rate, from hollow massive shells to inertial velocities.

nominations.title: Second-level termination of the PPT entanglement-cost hierarchy for two qutrits
nominations.authors: Wei Song, Xiao-Lan Zong, Ming Yang
nominations.abstract: We prove that for arbitrary two-qutrit quantum states, the semidefinite programming lower-bound hierarchy for the PPT entanglement cost terminates at the second level. Therefore, under operations preserving positive partial transpose, its zero-error asymptotic entanglement cost can be obtained by a semidefinite program involving only three Hermitian matrix variables. The key to the proof is to shorten the feasible dual chain by one level; to this end, we combine finite certificates verified by exact rational arithmetic with analytic estimates near the boundary of the parameter domain. This result shows that a unified terminating level exists for two-qutrit systems, whereas no unified terminating level exists for all dimensions.

nominations.title: Quantum simulation of real-time bosonic dynamics with binary and unary position encodings on superconducting and trapped-ion processors
nominations.authors: Masanori Hanada, Jiwoo Seo, Seok-Kyun Son, Junggi Yoon
nominations.abstract: Simulating a bosonic degree of freedom on qubit hardware requires discretizing its position space, and the qubit encoding of the resulting lattice determines the circuits that realize its real-time dynamics. We compare binary and unary encodings of a position lattice on superconducting (IBM) and trapped-ion (IonQ) processors. Binary encoding applies the kinetic term through the quantum Fourier transform; unary encoding uses one qubit per site, single-qubit rotations for the potential and excitation-conserving exchange gates for the kinetic term. For a single degree of freedom the unary dynamics is a free-fermion problem, and its product formula compresses exactly into a nearest-neighbor circuit of fixed size. With about two hundred two-qubit gates, these circuits resolve tunneling in a symmetric double well on both processors, with the right-well probability falling from 0.97 to 0.06 on IBM and from 0.96 to 0.12 on IonQ, whereas binary product-formula circuits with several thousand two-qubit gates do not reproduce the transfer. Noiseless emulation indicates that this contrast reflects the compilation as well as the encoding: without the fixed-size optimization, a unary product formula that captures the transfer also requires several thousand two-qubit gates. Post-selection on the single-excitation subspace removes leakage, and because every energy eigenstate of the symmetric grid populates both wells equally, the measured population reversal bounds the coherence between energy eigenstates from below.
